comments.author: icelancer
comments.story: Vintage video game cartridges with built-in modems
comments.text: It was. Very much so. I have a lot of fond memories of playing Kirby's Avalanche and Killer Instinct on the SNES over the phone lines. I could not fathom why more people didn't flock to the XBAND. It represented everything I ever wanted as a kid gamer. They had the right idea. Way before its time unfortunately, and shockingly. I still don't really understand why it didn't take off. Luckily, just last month (May 2019) there was a one hour documentary on it that covered a lot of the development of the unit. Well worth watching. [VIDEO]

comments.author: dimator
comments.story: A Closer Look at the Super NES Doom Source Code Release [video]
comments.why: XBAND retrospective, including runtime patching of games for lag
comments.text: There's an excellent retrospective on YouTube about the xband and how it was built. It was a product ahead of its time. For example, the way they got games that weren't built for laggy multiplayer to work was unbelievable: they recognized the cartridge and patched the code. Yes, that means every game that worked was a result of a custom built patching of that game's code at run time! [VIDEO]
